Forrest Bowers, Director

Doug Vincent-Lang, Commissioner

Kuskokwim Area Office Bethel, AK 99559

Juneau, AK 99811-5526

Advisory Announcement For Immediate Release: November 3, 2026 Time: 8:00 p.m.

CONTACT: Sam Decker and Madison Hardwig Kuskokwim Area Assistant Management Biologists (907) 459-7295 and (907) 459-7213

2026 Preliminary Kuskokwim Area Season Summary

This is an announcement from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (department) for fishers in the Kuskokwim Area.

Kuskokwim Area Management Kuskokwim River salmon fisheries were managed according to the Kuskokwim River Salmon Management Plan (5 AAC 07.365). The Kuskokwim Bay salmon fisheries were managed according to the Districts 4 and 5 Salmon Management Plan (5 AAC 07.367).

Kuskokwim River

Preseason Forecast The 2026 Kuskokwim River Chinook salmon forecast was for a range of 128,000 to 200,000 fish. The drainagewide Chinook salmon escapement goal is 65,000–120,000 fish (Table 1). If the run came back as projected, the drainage-wide and tributary escapement goals were expected to be achieved while providing for subsistence fishing opportunity. Chum salmon were predicted to come back near average, sockeye salmon above average and coho salmon at average run sizes, with escapement goals expected to be achieved and subsistence fishing opportunity provided. Preseason and inseason management decisions were made with input from the Kuskokwim River Salmon Management Working Group (Working Group). It was the intent of the department to manage all Kuskokwim River salmon stocks in a conservative manner, consistent with the Policy for the Management of Sustainable Salmon Fisheries under 5 AAC 39.222, to meet escapement goals and the subsistence priority.

Inseason Subsistence Management Beginning in 2011, federal special actions (FSA) have been approved by the Federal Subsistence Board, which have allowed for United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) to manage subsistence fisheries within the navigable waters adjacent to the Yukon Delta National Wildlife Refuge (Refuge). In 2026, the federal inseason manager requested and was granted a Temporary Special Action (TSA) which allowed up to 90 days of fisheries management and two Emergency Special Actions (ESA) which allowed for up to 60 days of management for Chinook, chum and coho salmon runs. The department managed subsistence fishing in the Kuskokwim Management area through May 31. The Refuge established TSA 1 effective in Sections 1–3 on June 1 and was intended to last until July 31. Under the Special Actions, inseason management decisions were made in partnership between the Refuge and the Kuskokwim River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission. USFWS will publish reports detailing their inseason management decisions.

The middle and upper portions of the Kuskokwim River (Sections 4 and 5) were managed by the department at all times of the year, as were the rivers in Kuskokwim Bay (Districts 4 and 5). The “Front-end closure”, designed to ensure lower river passage for upriver-bound Chinook salmon, began June 9 in Sections 4 and 5 and consisted of restricting gillnets in the mainstem. Selective gears were allowed during this salmon closure for important spring subsistence non-salmon harvest, primarily sheefish, pike and whitefish. With the gillnet closure came

1

2026 Kuskokwim Management Area Season Summary

additional restrictions, including mandatory release of Chinook salmon caught in selective gears and tributary closures. Due to continued low Chinook salmon returns to the Aniak River, specific actions were taken to further conserve that stock. The Aniak River and the “Aniak Box” (at the confluence with the mainstem Kuskokwim River) were closed to gillnets on June 11th and fishing for Chinook salmon remained closed until further notice.

The Working Group met and discussed harvest patterns and run timing with managers. Subsequently on June 12, fishing with gillnets was re-opened in Sections 4 and 5. Restrictions of 6-inch or less mesh size with a maximum length of 25 fathoms were put into place at the same time. Retention of all species was then allowed with selective gear in state waters. However, within the “Aniak box” and Aniak River subsistence fishing for Chinook salmon and gillnet gear remained closed.

Subsistence fisheries in Kuskokwim Bay were restricted to a mesh size of 6-inch or less to reduce Chinook salmon harvest while not limiting the harvest of other salmon species. Additionally, there is a regulation in District 4 that restricts fishing on Sundays between June 1 and July 15 and limits gear to 1 50-fathom net per boat, not exceeding 45 meshes in depth.

The chum salmon run came in stronger than predicted in 2026. Sonar passage of 175,109 fish through July 10, was above the 2018–2025 average of 108,877 fish. The Refuge then issued ESA 2, effective July 13 which relinquished mainstem management to the department but maintained Chinook salmon management authority in the tributaries within federal waters. On July 13, 90% of the Chinook salmon run had passed the sonar and the drainagewide escapement goal was expected to be achieved. Meanwhile, the Kuskokwim sonar project had counted 202,854 chum salmon, well above the average of 117,361 at that date. Additionally, 421,461 sockeye salmon had passed, which is less than the average passage of 599,457 (2018–2025). The department opened subsistence fishing with all gears for the harvest of chum and sockeye salmon. The first coho salmon was caught at the sonar on July 18th and as of August 5th 43,000 fish had passed the sonar site, well below the average of 106,500 coho salmon for that date. The department closed coho salmon fishing in Sections 1–3 on August 7th. Fishing for non-salmon remained open with selective gears and with gillnets in nonflowing waters and non-salmon spawning rivers upstream from 100 yards of the confluence with the mainstem Kuskokwim River. Subsequently, the Refuge issued ESA 3, which re-established management authority of Sections 1–3 and closed fishing from August 12–September 15. Due to the coho salmon conservation concern, working closely with the Working Group, the department closed subsistence fishing with gillnets in Section 4 for one week, Aug 21-28 and in Section 5 for one week, from Aug 28-Sept 4th. On September 15th the Refuge relinquished management authority back to the department. On September 18th the department relinquished all subsistence fishing restrictions from the mouth of the Kuskokwim River to the headwaters, and subsistence fishing opened for all species with all gears.

Post-season subsistence harvest surveys, previously funded by OSM and conducted by the department’s Subsistence Division, are not operating this year due to loss of funding.

2026 District 1 Commercial Fishery There were no commercial buyers or processors operating in the Kuskokwim River in 2026. While the chum and sockeye runs were strong, the Chinook and coho salmon run strength were below average and subsistence harvests were limited. Therefore, the department was unable to offer commercial harvest opportunity.

Kuskokwim River Sonar The department utilized the Kuskokwim River sonar to inform in-season management decisions. The sonar operated from June 3–August 25 and provided timely information about the abundance of salmon and whitefish species as they migrated up the Kuskokwim River. A test fishery was operated for species apportionment using a series of 6 gillnet mesh sizes: 8 1/2”, 7 1/2”, 6 1/2”, 5 1/4”, 4”, and 2 3/4” mesh. The sonar program generated daily species-specific passage estimates using species apportionment and sonar counts. The sonar passage

2

2026 Kuskokwim Management Area Season Summary

estimates (Table 2) are neither total abundance nor escapement estimates since some spawning occurs below the sonar and harvest occurs both downriver and upriver from the sonar.

Run Timing and Passage Estimates Chinook Salmon The estimated midpoint of the Chinook salmon run was June 27 (4 days later than average). The cumulative Chinook salmon passage estimate at the sonar was approximately 96,000 fish (95% CI: 84,000–108,000).

Sockeye Salmon The estimated midpoint of the sockeye salmon run was July 4 (5 days later than average). The cumulative sockeye salmon passage estimate at the sonar was approximately 498,000 fish (95% CI = 467,000–530,000).

Chum Salmon The estimated midpoint of the chum salmon run was July 15 (9 days later than average). The cumulative chum salmon passage estimate at the sonar was approximately 558,000 fish (95% CI = 512,000–604,000).

Coho Salmon The estimated midpoint of the coho salmon run was August 9 (8 days earlier than average). The final count of coho salmon past the sonar was approximately 164,000 (95% CI = 93,000–236,000).

Whitefish Five species of whitefish were assessed at the Kuskokwim River sonar (least and Bering cisco, broad and humpback whitefish, and sheefish). The cumulative cisco (least and Bering) passage estimate at the sonar was approximately 825,000 fish (95% CI: 726,000–924,000). The cumulative broad whitefish passage estimate at the sonar was approximately 13,000 fish (95% CI: 0,000–49,000). The cumulative humpback whitefish passage estimate at the sonar was approximately 389,000 fish (95% CI: 322,000–457,000). The cumulative sheefish passage estimate at the sonar was approximately 42,000 fish (95% CI: 34,000–50,000).

Salmon Escapement – Kuskokwim River Drainage Chinook Salmon A run reconstruction model is used to estimate the Kuskokwim River total run and escapement for Chinook salmon. The preliminary total run estimate is 117,811 (95% CI: 105,728–129,893) and an estimated 87,251 (95% CI: 75,168–99,333) Chinook salmon escaped Kuskokwim River fisheries, which met the drainagewide Sustainable Escapement Goal (SEG) range of 65,000–120,000 fish. Chinook salmon escapement was estimated at 1 weir in 2026 (Table 3). Escapement at the Kogrukluk River weir was 3,231 Chinook salmon, which fell below the SEG range of 4,800–8,800 fish. Seven aerial surveys were successfully carried out for Chinook salmon in 2026 (Table 4). The Chinook salmon aerial survey estimate at the Salmon (Pitka Fork) River was 789 fish, which fell within the SEG range of 470–1,600 fish.

Sockeye Salmon Sockeye salmon escapement was estimated at 2 weirs in 2026 (Table 5). Escapement at the Kogrukluk River weir was 3,992 sockeye salmon, which fell below the SEG range of 4,400–17,000 fish. Escapement at the Telaquana River weir was 89,124 sockeye salmon. No aerial surveys are conducted for sockeye salmon in the Kuskokwim River.

Chum Salmon Chum salmon escapement was estimated at 1 weir in 2026 (Table 6). Escapement at the Kogrukluk River weir was 11,362 chum salmon, which fell below the SEG range of 15,000–49,000 fish. No aerial surveys are conducted for chum salmon in the Kuskokwim River.

Coho Salmon

3

2026 Kuskokwim Management Area Season Summary

Coho salmon escapement was not estimated in 2026 due to extended periods of missed passage at the weir projects. Historical coho salmon escapement data can be found in (Table 7).s

Kuskokwim Bay

District 4 Quinhagak, Salmon Escapement

An aerial survey was flown for the Kanektok River on July 30th. The survey was flown within the standardized peak spawning abundance range of July 22 to August 5 and salmon observed demonstrated coloration and redd development in accordance to peak spawn timing. Conditions were ideal for an aerial survey and the survey was rated as good. 55,260 sockeye salmon were counted (Table 8), which exceeded the aerial survey SEG range of 15,300-41,000 fish. The Chinook salmon survey was rated the same and the Chinook salmon aerial survey SEG (range 3,900-12,000 fish) was achieved with a count of 4,968 fish (Table 8).

District 5 Goodnews Bay, Salmon Escapement

The North Fork Goodnews River aerial survey was flown on July 30th and weather conditions were optimal, thus the survey was rated as good. The survey was flown during standardized peak spawning abundance, though still considered an index of escapement. The sockeye salmon SEG of 9,600-18,000 was exceeded with 50,344 fish counted (Table 9). The Chinook salmon aerial SEG range of 640-3,300 fish was exceeded with a count of 3,541 fish.

Districts 4 and 5, Commercial Fishery

The 2026 Kuskokwim Bay commercial fishery began on July 7 and ended on July 31 for both District 4 and District 5. The commercial fishers were from the local communities with some fishing opportunities to coastal community members affected by Typhoon Halong. The target species was sockeye salmon. Incidentally caught species could be retained by fishers for personal use. The Bethel Community Services Foundation purchased incidentally caught salmon, Chinook and chum salmon, for their food bank protein boxes. Due to fewer than three registered processors in Districts 4 and 5, commercial harvest data is confidential for the 2026 season, however the historical data is presented in Tables 10 and 11.

District 4 Quinhagak

There were 20 commercial salmon fishing periods. The commercial fishing season was delayed from the historical start of June 15 to allow for Chinook salmon escapement. Additionally, for the first two periods, area closures were enacted near the mouth of the Kanektok River to allow for Chinook salmon escapement (Figure 1).

District 5 Goodnews Bay

There were 21 commercial fishing periods. The commercial season was delayed from the normal start of June 15 to allow for Chinook salmon escapement. Additionally, during the first two periods, area closures were enacted within Goodnews Bay to allow for Chinook salmon escapement (half district line, Figure 2).
